<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
The full picture is now clear.

Hero and Contact headings rely on static CSS glow without scroll animation. About section uses `useScrollGlow` for its stats and deploy text. The `.glow-text` class stays active because `text-gradient` relies on `text-transparent` and `background-clip: text`, which prevents the glow from fading on scroll.

The `text-shadow` on transparent text creates a glow around invisible letters, making the gradient appear dark and patchy. For the About section, `useScrollGlow` should override Tailwind colors via GSAP inline styles, but the initial state is set immediately on mount, so the text starts at dim green.

The dark text likely means ScrollTrigger never fired. The effect dependencies are stable, so the hook should initialize once on mount. The real question is whether `sectionRef.current` exists when the effect runs, since the section element may not yet be rendered before the child components attach their refs.

The ref should already be populated when the hook effect runs, since the section element is rendered before its children attach. The GSAP context is scoped correctly to the target element. The remaining concern is whether ScrollTrigger fires at all; if the section is already in view when the trigger initializes, the animation may not start.

GSAP inline styles override Tailwind classes, so the dim initial state should apply correctly. The real problem may be that ScrollTrigger needs a refresh after the Three.js hero causes layout shifts. The dark appearance of the gradient text is also caused by broken gradient rendering combined with `text-transparent`.

The fix plan is to remove the static `glow-text` class from the Hero and Contact headings and apply `useScrollGlow` to those sections instead. This requires extending the hook to support gradient text, since `color` cannot be animated on `text-transparent` elements. The existing approach of animating color will not work for these headings.

Gradient headings should animate opacity from 0.2 to 1 while using drop-shadow or text-shadow for the glow. Plain text in the About section should work if ScrollTrigger fires. The dim starting color is correct, so the failure likely lies in ScrollTrigger initialization.

Tailwind's `text-primary` utility might be marked `!important` in the config, which would block GSAP from overriding the color. The About section sits below the hero, so it should not be in view on initial load. The `fromTo` animation still applies its initial dim state immediately even when the element has not yet triggered.

The fix is to extend `useScrollGlow` with a `gradient` mode that animates opacity and drop-shadow for `text-gradient` elements, while keeping the default mode for plain text. The static `glow-text` class should be removed from Hero and Contact headings entirely, letting GSAP handle both the fade and the glow. The `.glow-text` CSS should be stripped down to an initial state or deleted so it does not clash with the scroll animation.

Gradient headings should start at 0.25 opacity with no glow and finish at full opacity with a drop-shadow glow. ScrollTrigger may need a refresh after fonts and images load. A potential bug was spotted in `useScrollGlow`: the trigger resolves from `triggerRef.current` or falls back to the element itself, but the effect dependencies do not guard against the trigger ref being missing when the hook mounts.

The fallback trigger resolves to the element itself when the ref is null, so individual stats still animate correctly. ScrollTrigger.refresh() should run after fonts and images load. Gradient headings must use only `text-gradient` without the static `glow-text` class.

GSAP will animate opacity from 0.2 to 1 and apply a drop-shadow glow. The About section should lose its `text-primary` Tailwind class so GSAP can drive the color entirely. The inline dim color should override Tailwind, but another factor may still be blocking the animation.

The `.glow-text` class is confirmed to be the culprit on Hero and Contact headings, since those elements carry it while About does not. GSAP `from` values are applied before the scroll trigger fires, so the dim initial state should render immediately. The next step is to add a `variant` option to `useScrollGlow`—either `'gradient'` or `'solid'`—so the hook can handle both transparent gradient text and plain text separately.

The concrete implementation is now clear. The Hero and Contact headings will lose the static `glow-text` class and receive `useScrollGlow` with a new `gradient` variant. The CSS utility will be reduced to an initial dim state or removed entirely. The About section will get a `ScrollTrigger.refresh()` call to recover from layout shifts. For gradient text, the animation will fade opacity from 0.2 to 1 while building up a layered drop-shadow glow.

A critical flaw surfaced: drop-shadow filters create hollow black centers on gradient text, which is why the previous approach was reverted. For gradient headings, the viable paths are now limited. The simplest route is to animate opacity alone and let a parent box-shadow provide the glow. Other options—pseudo-elements, background-position changes, or switching to solid color text—were considered too complex or too destructive.

The hollow black center occurs when drop-shadow filters are applied directly to the gradient text element. For gradient headings, the safest path is to animate only opacity and let a parent wrapper provide the glow. A wrapper-based approach with separate inner and outer spans, or a CSS `::before` pseudo-element toggled by GSAP, are the remaining alternatives.

Drop-shadow filters on gradient text leave hollow centers because they shadow the transparent alpha shape. Wrapping the text in a container or duplicating it behind the gradient would not solve the problem. The chosen fix is to animate only opacity from 0.25 to 1 on scroll. The static `glow-text` class will be removed from the Hero and Contact headings entirely.

The author briefly considered removing `text-transparent` from gradient text so GSAP could animate color directly, but rejected it because the user specifically wants the gradient-plus-glow effect. Solid text animations remain the safe choice for the About section.

A two-layer approach is now preferred for gradient headings. An absolute, blurred, low-opacity duplicate layer will sit behind the gradient text, and GSAP will animate that layer’s opacity to create the glow. This avoids the hollow-center issue that drop-shadow filters cause on transparent gradient fills.

The two-layer duplicate approach was abandoned as too complex. The simpler plan is to wire `useScrollGlow` directly onto the Hero and Contact headings, using a gradient-only opacity animation. The static `glow-text` class will be removed entirely, and the `.glow-text` CSS rule will be deleted or reduced so GSAP controls the final glow state. The About section will also be fixed if its solid-text animation is currently broken.

Chrome renders buggy text-shadows on clipped gradient text. The minimum viable fix is to start gradient headings at `opacity-20` and animate them fully opaque on scroll, dropping the static `glow-text` class entirely. A wrapper-level glow via `box-shadow` was dismissed because it cannot follow the text shape. The hook will be extended with a `mode` prop: `solid` for color and text-shadow, and `gradient` for opacity-only fade.

The Hero heading is already visible on page load, so its glow should likely fire on initial appearance rather than waiting for a scroll event. The existing entrance animation already moves it downward, but it never brightens. Solid text elements may also need their final text-shadow driven by GSAP instead of a static CSS class.

The Hero heading sits at the top of the viewport, so a `top 85%` scroll trigger would fire instantly on mount. The author is verifying whether ScrollTrigger treats that as already passed, which would prevent the glow from animating.

ScrollTrigger's `start: "top 85%"` waits until the element's top edge reaches 85% of the viewport height. Since the Hero heading begins at the top of the page, its top edge is at 0%, so the trigger never fires on initial load. The element therefore stays in its dim `from` state and never brightens on scroll.

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
The heading animation and dark glow CSS are now clear.

The About section already animates correctly. Hero and Contact headings stay permanently lit because they carry a static `.glow-text` class. I will remove that class from those sections and extend `useScrollGlow` to animate opacity and text-shadow on scroll.

Hero and Contact headings will use `useScrollGlow`. The Hero trigger needs care because the section is fully visible on page load. A `start` value of `"top 95%"` would fire instantly, so a delayed or timeline-based approach may be needed.

GSAP ScrollTrigger does not fire instantly on page load. The hero top sits at 0% of the viewport, below the 85% threshold, so the trigger waits until the user scrolls down. A different approach is needed for the Hero heading.

The hero heading cannot trigger a scroll animation at all. Because the hero section sits below the fold, its top edge starts far below the viewport and scrolls upward as the user scrolls down. The element never reaches the 85% viewport threshold, so the trigger never fires. This reveals a fundamental flaw in the current scroll animation approach.

Hero headings will use `start: "top top"` to brighten immediately on page load. Contact headings will keep `start: "top 85%"` since that section scrolls into view. The plan is ready.

I will add a `gradient` toggle to `useScrollGlow` so it can animate opacity and text-shadow together. The hook will also refresh ScrollTrigger and re-run when the trigger element mounts. Hero will use `gradient: true` with `start: "top top"` to brighten immediately on page load. Contact will use the same gradient mode.

The static `.glow-text` CSS will be removed entirely; GSAP will handle the glow alone. Gradient mode will animate opacity from 0.2 to 1 and text-shadow from none to the glow values. The Hero heading already has a GSAP timeline driving its y-position, so `useScrollGlow` can safely target the same element for opacity and shadow without conflict.

The static `.glow-text` CSS will be deleted entirely rather than kept for backwards compatibility. Other headings like Skills, Projects, and Experience do not carry the problematic class, so they will remain unchanged. The scroll glow fix will be limited to Hero, Contact, and the existing About section.

The user may be seeing the dimmed state before scrolling, or their ScrollTrigger may not be firing. The About stats already brighten correctly on scroll, and their staggered delay is intentional. The Contact heading will keep its existing y-axis animation separate from the new scroll glow hook.
</details></think>

Completely different approach now. Here's what changed:

**How it works:**
- `.text-gradient` starts with `background-position: 100%` — showing the dim/faded end of the gradient (12% opacity lime)
- When the parent gets `.revealed` (via `useReveal` IntersectionObserver), it transitions to `background-position: 0%` — sweeping the bright gradient in from left to right over 1.2s
- Stat cards with stagger delays inherit the delay via `.reveal-item .text-gradient`
- **Hero KHODABUX**: GSAP animates `backgroundPosition` directly (slides up while sweeping bright — no `opacity` on the gradient element at all)

**Why this works in Chrome:**
- Zero use of `opacity`, `filter`, or `text-shadow` on any `background-clip: text` element
- Only animates `background-position`, which Chrome handles perfectly
- Removed `.glow-text` entirely — no more cross-browser conflicts
